Software giants Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) are competing for dominance in the enterprise cloud market as businesses shift toward automated workflows. Deciding which stock is a better buy today requires a look at their evolving platforms.

Adobe provides essential tools for creative design and document management, while Salesforce leads the market for customer relationship management software. Both companies have integrated advanced artificial intelligence into their core offerings to drive growth. Investors often compare these two because they represent established leaders within the tech stocks sector with massive recurring revenue.

The case for Adobe

Adobe provides an end-to-end platform for creative, marketing, and document productivity professionals. Its solutions, including Adobe Acrobat, Creative Cloud, and the Adobe Experience Platform, are used by consumers and global enterprises. The company says it reaches 1 billion monthly active users across its various productivity and creativity solutions. Adobe leverages an extensive ecosystem of partner-integrated AI models to support its content workflows for students, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations.

In the fiscal year ended Nov. 28, 2025, revenue reached nearly $23.8 billion, which is a 10.5% increase over the previous year. This growth helped the company achieve a net income of approximately $7.1 billion, supporting its reputation among top tech stocks today. Adobe maintained a healthy net margin of roughly 30% during this period. This metric shows the percentage of each dollar of sales that the company retained as profit after accounting for all expenses.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.0x, meaning short-term assets are sufficient to cover short-term liabilities. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.6x, indicating that total debt is about 60% of shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Nov. 28, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $9.9 billion. Free cash flow is calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures and represents the cash a business generates after paying for its physical assets.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce provides customer relationship management technology and enterprise cloud solutions through its Agentforce and Customer 360 platforms. The company serves businesses using unified data and autonomous AI agents to connect with their customers. Its customer base spans organizations of all sizes across industries like financial services and retail. Salesforce integrates data management via its recent acquisition of Informatica and enhances its analytics through strategic acquisitions of smaller firms.

Arista Networks vs. Salesforce: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Jake Lerch, The Motley Fool

CRM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Deciding between high-growth infrastructure and steady software giants is a classic investor dilemma. Here is how Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stack up for your 2026 investment strategy.

Arista Networks provides the physical backbone for massive data centers, while Salesforce offers the digital tools businesses use to manage their customers. Both companies are deeply integrated into their respective technology markets, but they offer vastly different ways to play the ongoing digital transformation of the global economy.

The case for Arista Networks

Arista Networks designs high-speed networking hardware and software tailored for large-scale data centers and campus environments. Its business strategy centers on the Ethernet market, specifically targeting "Cloud Titans" and specialty providers building out artificial intelligence infrastructure. Because the company historically relied on significant purchases from a small number of large customers, this revenue concentration adds a layer of risk to the business even as it expands. This expansion is particularly visible in the growing market for tech stocks that support AI infrastructure.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached nearly $9.0 billion. This represented a growth rate of approximately 28.6% over the prior fiscal year, driven by strong demand for high-capacity networking ports. The company also maintained strong profitability during this period, reporting net income of close to $3.5 billion. Its net margin of roughly 39% reflects a competitive position in a hardware market often characterized by high barriers to entry and specialized engineering requirements.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x, indicating it has no total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 3.0x, meaning the company holds three times as many current assets as current liabilities to cover its short-term obligations. Free cash flow, which is the cash remaining after paying for operating costs and capital expenditures, reached nearly $4.3 billion for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce dominates the enterprise software landscape through its integrated platform that combines data, applications, and artificial intelligence. Its current strategy focuses on the Agentforce 360 platform, which enables organizations to deploy autonomous AI agents across their sales and service departments. Unlike hardware companies that may rely on a few large buyers, no single customer accounts for more than 10% of Salesforce's total revenue. This provides a diversified revenue base as the company shifts from selling traditional software subscriptions to usage-based AI services.

title: Salesforce vs. Snowflake: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Salesforce vs. Snowflake: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

SNOW

Trading disclosure

Choosing between Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) requires weighing steady profitability against explosive revenue growth. Both companies are essential players in the modern data economy but offer very different investment profiles.

Salesforce focuses on helping companies manage customer relationships through a suite of integrated software tools. Snowflake provides a cloud-native platform that allows organizations to consolidate and analyze vast amounts of data, often serving as the foundation for enterprise AI strategies.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce operates as a dominant force in the tech stocks landscape, providing software that manages sales, service, and marketing on a single platform. The company recently pivoted toward agentic AI through its Agentforce platform, which allows businesses to deploy autonomous digital workers. It serves a massive global customer base and has expanded its capabilities by acquiring data management firms like Informatica and integrating them into its core ecosystem.

In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 9.6% over the prior year. The company demonstrated significant bottom-line improvement, reporting net income of close to $7.5 billion. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 18%, as Salesforce continues to focus on balancing expansion with disciplined expense management.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x, which measures total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, comparing current assets to liabilities, was roughly 0.8x. Free cash flow, calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached close to $14.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Snowflake

Snowflake provides the AI Data Cloud, a platform that enables organizations to store and process data across different cloud providers. Its consumption-based model means customers pay for the resources they actually use, which appeals to businesses looking for flexibility. By early 2026, the company served over 800 of the Forbes Global 2000, emphasizing its importance to large-scale enterprises that require high-performance data engineering and analytics.

In FY 2026, revenue reached approximately $4.7 billion, showing robust growth of roughly 29.2% compared to the previous year. Despite this rapid top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of close to $1.3 billion. This produced a net margin of roughly -28.4%, illustrating that the business is still heavily prioritizing market share gains and research over immediate GAAP profitability.

title: Why Braze Stock Soared This Week

Why Braze Stock Soared This Week
Anders Bylund, The Motley Fool

^GSPC
CRM

Trading disclosure

A $5.66 billion cash buyout offer from cloud giant Salesforce (NYSE: CRM) sent customer engagement software maker Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE) soaring 56.3% this week.

Braze stock changed hands at $45.86 as of the close on Thursday, Oct. 22, up 56.3% from Friday, Oct. 16's close through Thursday, Oct. 22's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) was flat, and the Nasdaq-100 was down 0.8%.

Salesforce strikes a $5.66 billion deal for Braze

Announced Tuesday, Oct. 20, the definitive agreement gives Braze Class A shareholders $47.50 per share in cash, representing a 58% premium over its $30.04 closing price on Oct. 19. The $5.66 billion enterprise valuation delivers an immediate cash outcome for shareholders following a prolonged period of industrywide valuation compression in software. Under the terms, Salesforce will absorb the entire business, while Braze's chief executive officer, Bill Magnuson, and the core leadership team will transition to Salesforce post-closing.

Braze sells cloud-based customer engagement software, allowing consumer brands to automate personalized messaging across mobile apps, email, and text to enterprise marketers. Its technology coordinates real-time communications for high-profile clients like Canva, Instacart, Urban Outfitters, and Venmo. In its last reported quarter ended July 31, 2026, the company generated $227.2 million in revenue, up 26.2% year over year, demonstrating steady expansion across enterprise accounts.

Because this is an all-cash takeover at a fixed price, traditional valuation multiples like price-to-sales no longer govern the stock's daily movements. Instead, Braze now trades on merger-arbitrage dynamics, at $45.86 per share -- slightly below the $47.50 buyout offer to reflect transaction timing and regulatory closing conditions. This week's definitive buyout agreement flips the investment case from a long-term growth play into a short-term merger arbitrage bet.

Image source: Getty Images.

What's next for Braze

The acquisition is expected to close during Salesforce's fiscal year 2028, which spans February 2027 through January 2028. Completion remains subject to customary closing conditions, including required regulatory clearances and a vote by Braze shareholders. The merger disclosure also specifies financial protections, including a $300 million regulatory failure fee payable by Salesforce and a $191 million breakup fee if Braze accepts a superior proposal.

For current investors, attention shifts entirely from quarterly operational execution to deal completion mechanics. If the acquisition closes as planned, shareholders will receive the $47.50 cash payout per share. However, if regulatory bodies or unforeseen obstacles break the deal, the stock faces downside risk back toward its pre-announcement trading level near $30.

Most of the gain, about 77.2%, comes from Salesforce growing revenue. Trefis models revenue growing 9.5% a year in the scenario. That sits below the 11.2% Salesforce delivered over the twelve months to July 2026. Trefis uses 85% of that recent pace because the latest year ran more than a tenth above the 9.3% average of the two years before it.

The Salesforce Businesses That Have To Keep Growing

For that revenue gain to arrive, the faster parts of Salesforce have to keep outgrowing the slower ones. On the August 26, 2026 call, management said revenue rose 11% in fiscal Q2 2027, driven by Slack and Agentforce.

Management also said annual recurring revenue from Agentforce reached $1.5 billion and customer attrition was near its lowest level ever. The company's fiscal 2027 revenue guide of $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion represents about 11.4% growth. That runs about 2 percentage points ahead of the scenario's yearly pace.

title: Could You Have Seen The Run In Microsoft Stock Coming?

Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 36.8% from July 24 to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. This rally followed a period where the shares had lost 17.7% over the six months before July 24. By the end of this run, investors were paying a much higher price for the same twelve months of Microsoft's earnings. What had Microsoft told investors before July 24?

What Microsoft Told Investors Before July 24

Well over a year before the run, management told investors that customers were buying more. On its January 29, 2025 call, management said large companies were beginning to move from small trials to "enterprise-wide deployments", and that commercial bookings, the contracts customers sign for future sales, had increased 67%, a jump the finance chief said was driven by Azure commitments from OpenAI.

Six months later, on the July 30, 2025 call, management said Azure, its cloud platform, had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%. This expansion was more than twice the 14.9% growth Microsoft reported as a whole for fiscal 2025.

Company filings reinforced these statements. Microsoft's revenue growth from a year earlier rose from 13.3% in the quarter ended March 2025 to 18.1% in the quarter ended June 2025. Growth was still 18.3% in the quarter ended March 2026, which Microsoft filed on April 29, 2026, before the run. The evidence was public and held steady, but the shares still lost 17.7% in the six months before July 24.

How Much More Investors Now Pay For Microsoft's Earnings

At the October 22 close, investors paid 28.9 times Microsoft's earnings for the twelve months to June 2026, against 20.7 times at the end of June. The end-of-June multiple was the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2017.

The business maintained the pace shown in its earlier filings. In the quarter ended June 2026, Microsoft's revenue was $90.0 billion, up 17.7% from a year earlier. The shares rose 15.5% on July 30, 2026, marking the biggest one-day move of the run.

Microsoft's performance diverged notably from its mega-cap peers over this three-month span. Alphabet, Amazon and Apple stock each returned 7.9% or less over the same three months.

Is Microsoft Still Growing At The Same Pace?

On sales, yes. Microsoft's revenue grew between 16.7% and 18.4% from a year earlier in each of the four quarters to June 2026, much the same pace the filings showed before the run.

Profit on each dollar of those sales has slipped, however. Microsoft's operating margin fell in each of the last three quarters, dropping from 48.9% in the quarter ended September 2025 to 45.1% in the quarter ended June 2026. This figure remained above the 44.9% of a year earlier. Over the full twelve months, the margin was still 46.8%, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company.
